title: How Codex Works — Dominik Kundel, OpenAI

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 92%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Codex is a developer platform—the harness, protocols, and APIs are infrastructure that other engineers build on, and the talk emphasizes the open ecosystem and third-party builds.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: Codex is specifically a coding agent with file editing, shell access, and apply patch tools, making it a coding assistant as a primary use case.

domains.rationale: The talk explicitly states the harness is open and most features live in the responses API so others can borrow them, indicating the architecture applies beyond coding to general agent use.

summary: Dominik Kundel presents 'Codex, Behind the Harness' at AI Engineer World's Fair, detailing the architecture of OpenAI's open-source coding agent harness. The harness is Apache 2 licensed, written in Rust (codex-rs), and powered by two open protocols: the app server protocol (connecting UI to harness) and the Responses API (connecting harness to inference), both designed for an open ecosystem supporting third-party builds. The talk covers context construction balancing size, flexibility, and cachability; deferred tools surfaced via tool search rather than entering context; available skills capped at 2% of the context window with progressive description trimming; and async actions using a spawn agent tool with send input, wait, and shutdown capabilities. Computer use evolved from one-action-at-a-time to code execution where the agent scripts interactions in JavaScript or Python. Browser use runs through a persistent Node REPL writing Playwright code across turns. File editing uses an apply patch tool (models trained on it since GPT-5) and a shell tool where the model naturally uses ripgrep. Cross-platform sandboxing uses Seatbelt (macOS), Bubblewrap (Linux), and a custom open-source Windows sandbox. Auto review subagents address approval fatigue: when the model escalates, a read-only subagent with no spawning ability judges the action against the transcript and user authorization context. GPT 5.3 Codex Spark on Cerebras at 1,000 tokens/sec made inference no longer the bottleneck—the network was—prompting WebSocket mode, which replaces SSE over HTTP with a persistent stateful connection sending only changed data per turn. Long-horizon goals use continuation prompt injection until the model calls an update goal tool, favoring concrete verifiable objectives. Auto compaction (manual or automatic, server-side, model-trained) compresses the context window for long-running sessions.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent production agent harness architecture where each component addresses a specific bottleneck or tension in building real-world AI agents. The two protocols (app server and Responses API) establish the open interfaces that make the system extensible. Context construction, deferred tools, and the 2% skills cap manage the fundamental trade-off between giving the model enough information and preserving cache efficiency. The action layer—spawn agent, code execution, browser use via REPL, apply patch, and shell—provides the agent with increasingly expressive capabilities while maintaining safety through cross-platform sandboxing. Auto review subagents bridge the gap between security and usability by providing intelligent automated approval judgment. WebSocket mode and stateful context address the network bottleneck that emerged when Cerebras-accelerated inference reached 1,000 tokens/sec. Goal continuation loops and auto compaction enable long-running autonomous sessions. Together, these concepts illustrate how a production agent system must optimize across multiple layers simultaneously—context, tools, safety, transport, and session management—to move beyond toy demos to reliable autonomous coding agents. The open-source nature of the implementation (Apache-2.0, Rust in codex-rs) makes these patterns directly studyable and reusable.
temporalContext: This video was published on 2026-08-10 at AI Engineer World's Fair, with research conducted as of 2026-08-23. The talk references GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark (released 2026-02-12), GPT-5.4 tool search capabilities, and models trained on apply patch since GPT-5. The openai/codex repository has been public since 2025-04-13, and the Responses API was introduced 2025-03-11. The speaker notes that 'things change quickly with new model releases and new APIs,' so some implementation details may have evolved between the talk date and research date.

concepts.name: Responses API
concepts.explanation: An agentic rethinking of chat completions with built-in capabilities like web search and image generation. It connects the harness to the inference layer and is being standardized with partners (Ollama, LM Studio, Nvidia).
concepts.importance: This is one of the two foundational protocols powering Codex and represents a shift from chat-oriented APIs to agent-oriented APIs, making it a reference architecture for the industry.

concepts.name: Context Construction
concepts.explanation: The process of assembling what enters the model's context window, balancing three concerns: size (minimizing token usage), flexibility (supporting diverse tool registries and skills), and cachability (keeping the prefix stable so KV cache can be reused).
concepts.importance: Context construction is arguably the most important step in the agent loop—it determines what the model can see and act on, directly affecting agent performance and cost.

concepts.name: Deferred Tools and Tool Search
concepts.explanation: Rather than loading all tool definitions into context upfront, deferred tools are surfaced via a tool search mechanism where the model dynamically searches for and loads tools at runtime. Available in the Responses API since GPT-5.4.
concepts.importance: This preserves model cache and reduces token usage while maintaining access to a large tool registry, solving the tension between tool availability and context efficiency.

concepts.name: Available Skills Cap (2%)
concepts.explanation: The list of available skills is capped at 2% of the total context window. When the list grows, descriptions are progressively trimmed to stay within the cap.
concepts.importance: This is a concrete strategy for managing context budget allocation between skills and other content, ensuring the model always has room for actual task context.

concepts.name: Spawn Agent Tool
concepts.explanation: A tool that allows the agent to create new agent instances with send input, wait, and shutdown capabilities. This powers async actions and background terminals.
concepts.importance: This is a multi-agent coordination primitive that enables concurrent task execution, making it possible for the agent to manage parallel workflows.

concepts.name: Code Execution for Computer Use
concepts.explanation: Computer use evolved from one-action-at-a-time (e.g., click, type) to code execution where the agent scripts its own interactions in JavaScript or Python, enabling more complex and composable automation.
concepts.importance: This shift from discrete actions to programmable interactions dramatically increases the expressiveness and reliability of computer use, moving from brittle step-by-step automation to scripted workflows.

concepts.name: Auto Review Subagent
concepts.explanation: When the model escalates an action for approval, a separate read-only subagent with no spawning ability judges the action against the transcript and user authorization context. It distinguishes explicitly requested actions from touching unmentioned resources.
concepts.importance: This pattern addresses approval fatigue—the tendency for users to grant blanket full access to avoid repeated approval prompts—by providing intelligent, context-aware automated judgment.

concepts.name: Approval Fatigue
concepts.explanation: The problem where repeated approval prompts push users toward granting full access, which security teams dislike. Auto review subagents mitigate this by providing intelligent automated judgment for escalated actions.
concepts.importance: Approval fatigue is a critical UX-security tension in production agent systems; understanding it is essential for designing agent permission systems that are both safe and usable.

concepts.name: Stateful Context via WebSocket
concepts.explanation: WebSocket mode enables stateful context where the server maintains context state across turns, so only changed items are transmitted rather than the full context with every request.
concepts.importance: This is a fundamental shift from stateless API calls to stateful agent sessions, reducing network overhead and enabling faster turn cycles at high inference speeds.

concepts.name: Goal Continuation Loops
concepts.explanation: When the model exhausts its turn on a long-horizon goal, the harness injects a continuation prompt containing the objective. This loops until the model calls an update goal tool. Concrete verifiable objectives are favored over essay-style goals.
concepts.importance: This pattern enables agents to pursue multi-step, long-running objectives that exceed a single inference turn, which is essential for autonomous coding tasks.

concepts.name: GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark on Cerebras
concepts.explanation: GPT 5.3 Codex Spark runs on Cerebras WSE-3 at 1,000 tokens per second, making inference no longer the bottleneck—the network became it. This performance shift motivated WebSocket mode.
concepts.importance: This illustrates how hardware acceleration changes the optimization target for agent systems, shifting focus from inference latency to network transport efficiency.

concepts.name: Continuation Prompt Injection
concepts.explanation: The harness injects a continuation prompt including the user's objective when the model finishes its turn without completing the goal. The loop continues until the model explicitly calls an update goal tool.
concepts.importance: This is a practical implementation of persistent goal-directed behavior in LLM agents, bridging the gap between single-turn inference and multi-turn autonomous operation.

concepts.name: App Server Protocol
concepts.explanation: The protocol connecting the UI layer to the Codex harness, designed as an open interface that powers the Codex app and third-party projects (Theos T3 code, RemoteX, Cloud Code plugin, even Doom). It enables any client to drive the harness.
concepts.importance: This protocol is the primary integration point for building on top of Codex, making the harness extensible beyond OpenAI's own UI.

concepts.name: WebSocket Mode
concepts.explanation: Replaces SSE over HTTP with a persistent WebSocket connection carrying stateful context, so turns ship only changed data rather than resending every item. Demonstrated reducing transmitted items from 9 to 1 per turn.
concepts.importance: When inference speed reached 1,000 tokens/sec on Cerebras, the network became the bottleneck. WebSocket mode addresses this, making it a critical transport-layer optimization for production agent systems.

concepts.name: Cross-Platform Sandboxing
concepts.explanation: All agent interactions go through sandbox layers: Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap on Linux, and a custom open-source Windows sandbox the team built themselves. Each platform requires a different isolation mechanism.
concepts.importance: Sandboxing is the security boundary that allows the agent to execute shell commands and edit files without compromising the host system. The Windows custom build highlights the engineering cost of cross-platform safety.

concepts.name: Apply Patch Tool
concepts.explanation: A file editing mechanism using structured patch syntax. Models have been trained on the apply patch concept since GPT-5, making it a reliable file editing interface.
concepts.importance: Using a purpose-trained tool for file edits produces more reliable results than freeform text editing, reducing the error rate of agent-driven code changes.

concepts.name: Shell Tool with Ripgrep
concepts.explanation: The harness provides a shell tool where the model naturally uses ripgrep for searching files on macOS/Linux and PowerShell on Windows, enabling flexible file system exploration and manipulation.
concepts.importance: Shell access gives the agent general-purpose file system capabilities beyond structured tools, and ripgrep is fast enough to not bottleneck the agent loop.

concepts.name: Persistent Node REPL for Browser Use
concepts.explanation: Browser interactions run through a persistent Node REPL where the agent writes Playwright code that persists across turns, allowing it to reference browser tabs and state between actions.
concepts.importance: This pattern turns browser automation into a stateful programming task rather than discrete actions, enabling more complex multi-step browser workflows.

concepts.name: Background Terminals via Spawn Agent
concepts.explanation: Async actions use a spawn agent tool that creates new agent instances with send input, wait, and shutdown capabilities. The same pattern powers background terminals, allowing the agent to run long-running processes concurrently.
concepts.importance: This architecture allows the agent to manage multiple concurrent tasks (e.g., running a build while continuing other work) without blocking the main agent loop.

concepts.name: Codex-rs Rust Implementation
concepts.explanation: The harness core is written in Rust under the codex-rs directory in the openai/codex repository, licensed Apache-2.0. The talk also demonstrated a TypeScript reimplementation (Nano Codex) built from the same public repo code.
concepts.importance: The Rust implementation provides performance and memory safety for the harness core, while the TypeScript demo proves the architecture is portable and understandable enough to reimplement.

concepts.name: SSE over HTTP (Replaced Transport)
concepts.explanation: Server-side events over HTTP was the previous transport mechanism for the Responses API, which sent the full context with every turn. WebSocket mode replaced it to reduce network overhead.
concepts.importance: Understanding the prior approach clarifies why WebSocket mode was necessary and quantifies the network overhead problem at high inference speeds.

concepts.name: Auto Compaction
concepts.explanation: A server-side, model-trained mechanism for compressing the context window in long-running agent sessions. Available manually or automatically, it compresses context in a way the model was trained to understand.
concepts.importance: Enables agents to run for extended periods without exhausting the context window, which is essential for long-horizon coding tasks.

sections.title: Introduction and Protocols Overview
sections.summary: Kundel introduces the talk, notes the harness is Apache 2 and written in Rust, and covers the two protocols: app server (UI to harness) and responses API (harness to inference), both designed for an open ecosystem with third-party integrations.

sections.title: Context Construction
sections.summary: Covers size, flexibility, and cachability concerns. Model instructions are predictable, but tool registries and skills grow unpredictably. Deferred tools and a 2% skills cap with description trimming manage this. Tool search is available in the responses API since GPT-5.4.

sections.title: Actions: Async, Computer Use, File System
sections.summary: Covers async actions (spawn agent, background terminals), computer use evolving to code execution, browser use via persistent Node REPL with Playwright, and file system interactions via apply patch and shell with ripgrep/PowerShell, all through sandbox layers.

sections.title: Sandboxing and Auto Review
sections.summary: Reviews sandbox layers (Seatbelt, Bubblewrap, custom Windows sandbox) and addresses approval fatigue via auto review: when the model escalates, a read-only subagent with no spawning ability judges the action against the transcript, user authorization, and risk taxonomies. Deleting a requested file reads differently from deleting an unmentioned .git folder. Applies to file system actions and network calls.

sections.title: Speed, WebSocket Mode, Loops, and Compaction
sections.summary: GPT 5.3 Codex Spark on Cerebras at 1,000 tokens/sec made inference no longer the bottleneck—the network was. WebSocket mode replaces SSE over HTTP with a persistent stateful connection sending only changed data. Goal loops inject a continuation prompt until the model calls an update goal tool, favoring concrete verifiable objectives. Auto compaction (manual or automatic, server-side, model-trained) compresses the context window for long-running sessions. Closing takeaways: harness is open source, most standout features live in the responses API, and users should watch how both evolve.

organization.name: OpenAI
organization.summary: OpenAI is an AI research and deployment company headquartered in San Francisco, California, founded in 2015. The organization built and maintains the Codex coding agent harness, the subject of this talk. The speaker Dominik Kundel works on Developer Experience and SDKs at OpenAI. OpenAI develops frontier models (GPT-5, GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark), the Responses API, and maintains the open-source Codex repository (github.com/openai/codex) under Apache-2.0 license written in Rust.

technologies.label: Codex Harness
technologies.summary: OpenAI's open-source coding agent harness, written in Rust (codex-rs) and licensed Apache-2.0. The harness is the central system discussed throughout the talk, managing context construction (balancing size, flexibility, and cachability), goal continuation loops that inject continuation prompts until the model calls an update goal tool, and auto compaction for long-running sessions. It is powered by two open protocols: the app server protocol connecting UI to harness, and the Responses API connecting harness to inference. The talk demonstrated the architecture is portable via a TypeScript reimplementation called Nano Codex.
technologies.role: The Codex Harness is the primary subject of the entire talk. Dominik Kundel presents its architecture, design decisions, and implementation details across all sections of the presentation.

technologies.label: OpenAI Responses API
technologies.summary: The OpenAI Responses API is an agentic rethinking of chat completions that serves as one of the two open protocols powering Codex, connecting the harness to the inference layer. It provides built-in capabilities like web search and image generation, and supports tool types including tool search (deferred tools, available since GPT-5.4), apply patch (trained since GPT-5), and shell. The speaker emphasized that most of the harness's distinctive features live in the Responses API so others can borrow them. WebSocket mode, a transport optimization for the API, replaced SSE over HTTP to address the network bottleneck that emerged at 1,000 tokens/sec inference speed.
technologies.role: Central protocol discussed throughout the talk. The speaker describes it as an agentic rethinking of chat completions and highlights that it is being standardized with partners for an open ecosystem.

technologies.label: GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark on Cerebras
technologies.summary: GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark is a smaller version of GPT-5.3-Codex that runs on Cerebras WSE-3 at 1,000+ tokens per second. This dramatic inference speed made inference no longer the bottleneck for the Codex harness—the network became it—directly motivating the WebSocket mode transport optimization. The model has a 128k context window and is text-only at launch. The first-party OpenAI press release confirms WebSocket mode reduced roundtrip overhead by 80%, per-token overhead by 30%, and time-to-first-token by 50%.
technologies.role: Presented as the performance catalyst that shifted the optimization target from inference latency to network transport efficiency, directly motivating WebSocket mode.

technologies.label: Agent Sandboxing and Auto Review
technologies.summary: The Codex harness implements cross-platform sandboxing as its primary security boundary: Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap on Linux, and a custom open-source Windows sandbox the team built themselves. This sandboxing layer allows the agent to execute shell commands, edit files, and run code execution for computer use without compromising the host system. Complementing the sandbox, the auto review system addresses approval fatigue: when the model escalates an action, a read-only subagent with no spawning ability judges the action against the transcript and user authorization context, distinguishing an explicitly requested file deletion from touching an unmentioned .git folder. The spawn agent tool is the underlying primitive for both async actions and the constrained auto review subagent.
technologies.role: The safety and security architecture is a major section of the talk, covering sandboxing layers across all three platforms and the auto review subagent pattern for addressing approval fatigue in production agent systems.
